prompt: The client asks: "Which cost-cutting option should we pursue first?" Fact sheet: renegotiating suppliers saves $8M a year and takes 6 months; closing two plants saves $15M a year, takes 2 years and costs $20M up front; cutting marketing saves $5M but risks sales; the target is $10M of savings this year; the company has 5,000 employees. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Close the two plants first. At $15M a year they save the most, 50% above the $10M target, and the savings last.
options.feedback: It ignores timing: closures take 2 years and $20M up front, so they can't deliver this year's target.

options.text: Supplier talks and plant closures both have merit. The order should reflect how fast the board needs savings.
options.feedback: This never commits, even though the target is this year.

options.text: Start with supplier renegotiation. It saves $8M within 6 months with no up-front cost, most of this year's $10M target.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and backs it with what decides it: savings this year.

options.text: Cut marketing first. With 5,000 employees to protect, it saves $5M without a single layoff.
options.feedback: Headcount isn't the issue, and cutting marketing saves only $5M while risking sales.

explanation: Full answer: Start with supplier renegotiation. It saves $8M within 6 months with no up-front cost, most of this year's $10M target; plant closures save more but take 2 years and $20M up front. The main risk is that suppliers push back and savings fall short, so the next step is to start talks now and plan plant consolidation as a second phase. What would change the answer: supplier savings well below $8M, which would bring other quick options forward.
